title: Hash cons a toy node

tests.expr: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "x" [] in string_of_bool (a == b)
let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "y" [] in Printf.sprintf "%d %d" a.id b.id
let mk = create () in let x = mk "x" [] in let a = mk "add" [x; x] in let b = mk "add" [x; x] in string_of_bool (a == b)
let mk = create () in let x = mk "x" [] in let _ = mk "add" [x; x] in let _ = mk "add" [x; x] in string_of_int (mk "z" []).id
let mk = create () in let x = mk "x" [] in let y = mk "y" [] in string_of_bool (mk "add" [x; y] == mk "add" [y; x])
let m1 = create () in let m2 = create () in let _ = m1 "a" [] in string_of_int (m2 "b" []).id
let mk = create () in let x = mk "x" [] in string_of_bool (mk "neg" [x] == mk "neg" [x; x])
let mk = create () in let a = mk "add" [mk "x" []; mk "x" []] in let b = mk "add" [mk "x" []; mk "x" []] in string_of_bool (a == b && a.id = 1)
let mk = create () in let last = ref (mk "c" []) in for _ = 1 to 1000 do last := mk "s" [!last] done; string_of_int (mk "s" [mk "c" []]).id

hints: The shape: `let create () = let tbl = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in fun op src -> ...`. A function can return a function, and the one it returns still sees `tbl` and `next`.
Keep a `Hashtbl` and an id counter inside `create`, so each call gets its own. The key is the op plus the ids of the sources, because sources are already hash consed.
On a hit, return the stored node itself, not a copy, so `==` holds. Only bump the counter when you actually build a new node.
explain: Each `create ()` makes its own table and counter, so tables never share ids. The key `(op, source ids)` is enough because the sources were themselves hash consed: equal sources already have equal ids. Returning the stored record on a hit is what makes `make` give back the physically same node.
